newsitem.title: USA: Weather uncertain for Thursday landing of shuttle.
newsitem.headline: Weather uncertain for Thursday landing of shuttle.

text.p: Astronauts aboard the shuttle Columbia began making hasty preparations for a Thursday landing in Florida after the unexpected failure of a navigation tool.

But a NASA spokesman said on Wednesday night that cloudy skies and uncertain weather conditions in Florida could delay the planned return to Kennedy Space Centre, now set for 7:34 a.m. EST (1234 GMT).
Weather conditions were better at a back-up landing site at Edwards Air Force Base in California, spokesman Rob Navias said.

The five astronauts were ordered home a day early after a crucial piece of navigation equipment failed early on Wednesday and forecasters called for worsening weather at all three shuttle landing sites.

The decision to call the shuttle home 24 hours earlier than planned came after one of the orbiter's three navigation units stopped working, and after a stuck airlock hatch last weekend forced NASA to cancel two planned spacewalks. NASA engineers have been stumped by the hatch problem, which is the first such occurrence in the shuttle's 15-year history.
The latest technical problem knocked out one of the shuttle's three crucial navigation units, known as inertial measurement units.

"We would like to land the shuttle tomorrow in Florida," said flight director Wayne Hale. "If the weather dictates otherwise, we have options at Edwards Air Force Base (in California) or we can stay up several more days."
NASA managers said that Friday weather forecasts called for rainy, unstable weather in central Florida, and windy conditions at two back-up landing sites on the U.S. West Coast.

Although Hale said the main reason for the crew's early return was the weather, he acknowledged the two equipment problems also played a role. "They certainly indicate that you ought to button things up and be prepared to come down at the earliest opportunity," he said, referring to the stuck hatch and the broken navigation unit.
The astronauts planned to spend the night testing the spaceship's landing systems and packing their gear for the ride home.

The shuttle's stuck airlock hatch was expected to cause some anxiety when Columbia's cargo bay doors are scheduled to swing shut shortly before 4 a.m. EST (0900 GMT). In the unlikely event the doors fail to close properly, the astronauts would have to pry open the hatch and make a spacewalk to manually crank the doors.
Earlier on Wednesday, astronauts aboard the Columbia guided the shuttle through a tricky manoeuvre to retrieve an orbiting telescope.

Through a series of precise rocket burns and careful steering, the five-member crew flew within 40 feet (12 metres) Orfeus-Spas, a powerful German-made space telescope. The telescope had been flying in formation with Columbia since the crew released it on Nov. 19, shortly after the shuttle was launched from Kennedy Space Centre.
Astronauts Tom Jones and Tammy Jernigan used the shuttle's robot arm to slowly pluck the satellite from space at 3:26 a.m. EST (0826 GMT) and tuck it into the payload bay for the ride home.

Scientists on the ground hope to collect data from the ultraviolet telescope to learn more about the life cycle of stars, especially the gaseous, soupy matter that acts as a nursery for stars outside the earth's solar system. Preliminary data from the telescope showed it collected a total of 420 observations of nearly 150 objects in space, including Mars, Jupiter, Saturn and the earth's moon.

"It's been an overwhelming and unqualified success," said Ronald Polidan, a member of the team of scientists directing the Orfeus-Spas work. "We have seen a number of different objects that did not look like what we expected."
